claim: The GAL4/UAS system provides spatial control of transgene expression in Drosophila.
source: This system relies on a cloned or endogenous promoter to drive the expression of the yeast transcription factor GAL4, which can then bind to the UAS (upstream activating sequence) sites upstream of a transgene and activate its expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the Drosophila field and is cited in the manuscript.

claim: GAL80 antagonizes GAL4 by inhibiting its activation domain.
source: GAL4 activity can be regulated by GAL80, a protein which antagonises GAL4 by inhibiting its activation domain (Lue et al., 1987), and thus the ability of the GAL4 to induce transcript expression (Lee and Luo, 1999; Suster et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Temperature-sensitive GAL80 (GAL80ts) allows temporal control of GAL4-induced transgene expression.
source: The generation of a fly line that ubiquitously expressed a temperature-sensitive version of GAL80 (GAL80ts) (Matsumoto et al., 1978) was a significant advance for the field, as it allowed temporal control of GAL4-induced transgene expression (McGuire et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Temperature affects a wide range of physiological and behavioural traits in Drosophila.
source: Flies, as ectotherms, are highly dependent on their ambient temperature, which affects a wide range of physiological and behavioural traits (Abram et al., 2017). These include sleep (Beckwith and French, 2019), territorial success (Zamudio et al., 1995), lifespan (McCabe and Partridge, 1997), development rate (Danjuma et al., 2014), immunity (Hunt et al., 2016), metabolism (Schou et al., 2017), and even their microbiome (Moghadam et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The GeneSwitch system shows leaky expression in the absence of RU-486.
source: Furthermore, the system shows leaky expression in the absence of the drug (RU-486) (Poirier et al., 2008; Scialo et al., 2016), and RU-486 can cause behavioural changes (Li and Stavropoulos, 2016) and is dangerous to handle for pregnant women as it can cause termination of the pregnancy (Avrech et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: RU-486 can cause behavioural changes in Drosophila.
source: Furthermore, the system shows leaky expression in the absence of the drug (RU-486) (Poirier et al., 2008; Scialo et al., 2016), and RU-486 can cause behavioural changes (Li and Stavropoulos, 2016) and is dangerous to handle for pregnant women as it can cause termination of the pregnancy (Avrech et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: RU-486 is dangerous to handle for pregnant women as it can cause termination of pregnancy.
source: Furthermore, the system shows leaky expression in the absence of the drug (RU-486) (Poirier et al., 2008; Scialo et al., 2016), and RU-486 can cause behavioural changes (Li and Stavropoulos, 2016) and is dangerous to handle for pregnant women as it can cause termination of the pregnancy (Avrech et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The QF system is not compatible with existing GAL4 lines.
source: Quinic acid is non-toxic for flies, however, the drawback of this system is that it is not compatible with the vast collection of existing GAL4 lines.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The auxin-degron system involves auxin-dependent ubiquitination and degradation of proteins tagged with an auxin-inducible degron (AID) sequence.
source: The auxin-degron system, first identified in Arabidopsis, involves the auxin-dependent ubiquitination, and subsequent degradation, of proteins that are tagged with a specific auxin-inducible degron (AID) sequence (Dharmasiri et al., 2005; Dharmasiri and Estelle, 2002; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The auxin-degron system has been successfully employed in Drosophila.
source: Importantly, the auxin-degron system has been successfully employed in Drosophila (Chen et al., 2018; Trost et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: AGES is compatible with existing GAL4-driver lines.
source: This auxin-inducible gene expression system (AGES) is safe to handle, cheap, easy to prepare, provides tuneable and stringent (i.e. not leaky) expression, and most importantly, is compatible with the majority of existing GAL4-driver lines developed by the Drosophila community.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the manuscript.

claim: AGES uses shorter AID sequences (minimal degron of IAA17) than previously used in Drosophila.
source: We included shorter AID sequences (minimal degron of IAA17) than previously used in Drosophila (Trost et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and compared to previous work.

claim: Fusion of minimal AID to luciferase resulted in a fusion protein with short half-life (~10 min) in plants.
source: Fusion of this minimal AID to luciferase resulted in a fusion protein with short half-life in plants (~10 min) (Dreher et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana TIR1 (AtTIR1) with two point mutations can deplete nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins in C. elegans.
source: We also instead used Arabidopsis thaliana TIR1 (AtTIR1), which has two point mutations (improving affinity and auxin sensitivity) that can deplete nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins in C. elegans (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The P2A sequence encodes a self-cleaving peptide that works efficiently in Drosophila cell culture.
source: The P2A sequence between AtTIR1 and AID-tagged GAL80 encodes a self-cleaving peptide that is known to work efficiently in Drosophila cell culture (Daniels et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: At 5 and 10 mM auxin, GFP fluorescence is clearly detectable in the abdomen of live female flies after 24 hr.
source: At 5 and 10 mM, GFP fluorescence is clearly detectable in the abdomen of live female flies (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 10 mM auxin for 24 hr results in ~60% of the GFP fluorescence levels seen in the positive control.
source: Based on this assay, 10 mM for 24 hr results in ~60% of the GFP fluorescence levels seen in the positive control (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At 1 mM auxin there is no detectable GFP above background fluorescence.
source: At 1 mM there is no detectable GFP above background fluorescence, and the levels are indistinguishable from both the 0 mM and the negative control (lacking both the GAL4 driver and the UAS-nls-GFP).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 5 and 10 mM auxin show levels of GFP mRNA equivalent to the positive control.
source: Here, 5 and 10 mM show levels of mRNA equivalent to the positive control, while 0 mM showed no significant difference when compared with the negative control.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 0 mM auxin showed no significant difference in GFP mRNA levels when compared with the negative control.
source: Here, 5 and 10 mM show levels of mRNA equivalent to the positive control, while 0 mM showed no significant difference when compared with the negative control.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adult males eat less than females.
source: Adult males eat less than females (Wong et al., 2009), therefore, this will impact on auxin ingestion and possibly on transgene induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: GFP expression is reduced in males compared to females, but there is still robust induction.
source: Although reduced compared to females, there is still a robust induction of GFP expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 48 hr (24 hr without auxin), GFP levels were reduced.
source: At 48 hr (24 hr without auxin), GFP levels were reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: At 72 and 96 hr after auxin removal, GFP levels were not significantly different to 0 hr.
source: At 72 and 96 hr, the levels were not significantly different to 0 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: After 15 weeks at 4°C, auxin food can induce GFP levels to that of newly prepared food.
source: Even after 15 weeks, the auxin food could induce GFP levels to that of newly prepared food (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In larvae, expression can be induced at lower concentrations of auxin than in adults.
source: Here, we observed that expression could be induced at lower concentrations of auxin.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: When using food containing no auxin in larvae, there is no detectable GFP.
source: When using food containing no auxin, there is no detectable GFP, whereas with 1 mM auxin, GFP is expressed, although at lower levels than with higher concentrations of auxin (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: With 1 mM auxin in larvae, GFP is expressed, although at lower levels than with higher concentrations.
source: When using food containing no auxin, there is no detectable GFP, whereas with 1 mM auxin, GFP is expressed, although at lower levels than with higher concentrations of auxin (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Five mM auxin is an optimal concentration for larvae, as concentrations above that do not increase GFP levels.
source: Five mM auxin is an optimal concentration, as concentrations above that do not increase GFP levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Five mM auxin can induce low-level GFP expression in larvae after 6 hr.
source: Five mM auxin can induce low-level GFP expression after 6 hr (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: 18 hr is required to provide maximum levels of GFP expression in larvae with 5 mM auxin.
source: However, 18 hr is required to provide maximum levels of expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: NAA can cross the blood-brain barrier in Drosophila.
source: NAA can cross the blood-brain barrier in Drosophila (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: K-NAA auxin can cross the blood-brain barrier in Drosophila.
source: This demonstrates that AGES works in the central nervous system and that K-NAA auxin can cross the blood-brain barrier in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of GFP expression in the brain after K-NAA treatment.

claim: AGES works in the central nervous system.
source: This demonstrates that AGES works in the central nervous system and that K-NAA auxin can cross the blood-brain barrier in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing GFP expression in the brain.

claim: In the absence of auxin, there is no detectable GAL4 activity in Or85a-GAL4 and grh-GAL4 driver lines.
source: In both cases there was no detectable GAL4 activity in the absence of auxin, while in the presence of auxin (10 mM for adults and 5 mM for larvae) GFP in a pattern consistent with the GAL4 driver is observed (Figure 4A and C) at levels significantly above background fluorescence levels (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the presence of auxin (10 mM for adults and 5 mM for larvae), GFP in a pattern consistent with the GAL4 driver is observed in Or85a-GAL4 and grh-GAL4 driver lines.
source: In both cases there was no detectable GAL4 activity in the absence of auxin, while in the presence of auxin (10 mM for adults and 5 mM for larvae) GFP in a pattern consistent with the GAL4 driver is observed (Figure 4A and C) at levels significantly above background fluorescence levels (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Time to pupation (from egg-laying) is unaffected for auxin concentrations up to 5 mM.
source: Time to pupation (from egg-laying) is unaffected for concentrations up to 5 mM, however, 10 mM caused a delay of approximately 1 day (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 10 mM auxin caused a delay of approximately 1 day in time to pupation.
source: Time to pupation (from egg-laying) is unaffected for concentrations up to 5 mM, however, 10 mM caused a delay of approximately 1 day (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ten mM auxin causes some developmental delay, although it has no impact on the survival of the flies through developmental stages.
source: Ten mM auxin causes some developmental delay, although it has no impact on the survival of the flies through these developmental stages (compared to a no auxin control) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Concentrations of 5 and 10 mM auxin have no effect on adult survival and lifespan.
source: Survival assays on both male and female adults show that concentrations of 5 and 10 mM have no effect on survival and lifespan (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Auxin does not affect locomotion of larvae (crawling assay) at 5 mM.
source: We also tested whether auxin affects locomotion of larvae (crawling assay) and adults (climbing assay) and see no significant effects with 5 and 10 mM auxin, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Auxin does not affect locomotion of adults (climbing assay) at 10 mM.
source: We also tested whether auxin affects locomotion of larvae (crawling assay) and adults (climbing assay) and see no significant effects with 5 and 10 mM auxin, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The small ventrolateral neurons (sLNvs) are both necessary and sufficient for maintenance of free-running locomotor rhythms.
source: A key circuit for control of Drosophila rhythmic behaviour is the ventrolateral neuron (LNv) cluster, of which the small ventrolateral neurons (sLNvs) are both necessary and sufficient for maintenance of free-running locomotor rhythms (Grima et al., 2004; Renn et al., 1999; Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PDF is a key clock output neuropeptide required for synchronisation of clock neuron groups.
source: PDF is a key clock output neuropeotide required for synchronisation of clock neuron groups, and loss of PDF function results in arrythmicity, desynchronisation of clock oscillators, and altered period length (Lear et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2003; Sheeba et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of PDF function results in arrythmicity, desynchronisation of clock oscillators, and altered period length.
source: PDF is a key clock output neuropeotide required for synchronisation of clock neuron groups, and loss of PDF function results in arrythmicity, desynchronisation of clock oscillators, and altered period length (Lear et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2003; Sheeba et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Adult-specific silencing of PDF+ LNvs by expression of Kir2.1 using PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch is sufficient to nearly ablate circadian locomotor rhythms in constant conditions without resetting the molecular clock.
source: Adult-specific silencing of PDF+ LNvs by expression of the inwardly rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1 using PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch is sufficient to nearly ablate circadian locomotor rhythms in constant conditions without resetting the molecular clock (Depetris-Chauvin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: 2 mM NAA feeding is sufficient for AGES-induced expression of Kir2.1 in adult PDF+ clock neurons to ablate circadian locomotor behaviour.
source: In summary, we find that 2 mM NAA feeding is sufficient for AGES-induced expression of Kir2.1 in adult PDF+ clock neurons to ablate circadian locomotor behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A stronger ablation of locomotor rhythmicity was observed in the AGES compared to GeneSwitch.
source: Indeed, we observed a stronger ablation of locomotor rhythmicity in the AGES compared to GeneSwitch, with fewer off-target behavioural effects of NAA feeding of parental control flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: NAA feeding has fewer off-target behavioural effects on parental control flies compared to RU-486.
source: Indeed, we observed a stronger ablation of locomotor rhythmicity in the AGES compared to GeneSwitch, with fewer off-target behavioural effects of NAA feeding of parental control flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: 2 mM NAA feeding significantly lengthened the behavioural period of male PDF-GAL4/+; AGES/+ parental controls by 19 min.
source: Two mM NAA feeding significantly lengthened the behavioural period of male PDF-GAL4/+; AGES/+ parental controls by 19 min, with no effect on females of the same genotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: 2 mM NAA had no effect on the behavioural period of female PDF-GAL4/+; AGES/+ parental controls.
source: Two mM NAA feeding significantly lengthened the behavioural period of male PDF-GAL4/+; AGES/+ parental controls by 19 min, with no effect on females of the same genotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: 200 μg/mL RU-486 feeding reduced circadian locomotor rhythms in both sexes of flies with PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch-driven expression of Kir2.1.
source: In agreement with the classic study by Depetris-Chauvin et al., 2011, 200 μg/mL RU-486 feeding also reduced circadian locomotor rhythms in both sexes of flies with PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch-driven expression of Kir2.1 (Figure 6E and F), though the effect was not as strong as 2 mM NAA feeding in the AGES flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: The effect of RU-486 on circadian locomotor rhythms was not as strong as 2 mM NAA feeding in the AGES flies.
source: In agreement with the classic study by Depetris-Chauvin et al., 2011, 200 μg/mL RU-486 feeding also reduced circadian locomotor rhythms in both sexes of flies with PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch-driven expression of Kir2.1 (Figure 6E and F), though the effect was not as strong as 2 mM NAA feeding in the AGES flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: RU-486 feeding resulted in a broader distribution of locomotor rhythm strengths and a net increase in rhythmicity in male PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch parental control flies.
source: In addition, RU-486 feeding resulted in a broader distribution of locomotor rhythm strengths and a net increase in rhythmicity in male PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch parental control flies (Figure 6E), which was accompanied by a 51 min increased period length and increased average 24 hr locomotor activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2G.

claim: RU-486 feeding was accompanied by a 51 min increased period length in male PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch parental control flies.
source: In addition, RU-486 feeding resulted in a broader distribution of locomotor rhythm strengths and a net increase in rhythmicity in male PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch parental control flies (Figure 6E), which was accompanied by a 51 min increased period length and increased average 24 hr locomotor activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2G.

claim: RU-486 feeding increased average 24 hr locomotor activity in male PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch parental control flies.
source: In addition, RU-486 feeding resulted in a broader distribution of locomotor rhythm strengths and a net increase in rhythmicity in male PDF-GAL4-GeneSwitch parental control flies (Figure 6E), which was accompanied by a 51 min increased period length and increased average 24 hr locomotor activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2G.

claim: RU-486 increased the period of female PDF-Gal4-GeneSwitch parental controls by 46 min.
source: RU-486 also increased the period of female PDF-Gal4-GeneSwitch parental controls by 46 min, with no effect on total activity or rhythm strength (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2F,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2F,H.

claim: RU-486 had no effect on total activity or rhythm strength in female PDF-Gal4-GeneSwitch parental controls.
source: RU-486 also increased the period of female PDF-Gal4-GeneSwitch parental controls by 46 min, with no effect on total activity or rhythm strength (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2F,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2F,H.

claim: AGES eliminates the need for temperature shifts to manipulate temporal expression.
source: Here, we present AGES, an auxin-inducible gene expression system, which eliminates the need for temperature shifts to manipulate temporal expression and lacks many of the drawbacks of the current drug-inducible systems.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the manuscript.

claim: AGES lacks many of the drawbacks of the current drug-inducible systems.
source: Here, we present AGES, an auxin-inducible gene expression system, which eliminates the need for temperature shifts to manipulate temporal expression and lacks many of the drawbacks of the current drug-inducible systems.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the manuscript.

claim: A significant benefit of AGES over existing systems is its compatibility with most existing GAL4-driver lines.
source: A significant benefit of AGES over existing systems is its compatibility with most existing GAL4-driver lines.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the manuscript.

claim: AGES uses a GAL80 fusion protein, which allows the use of the system alongside the majority of existing GAL4-driver lines.
source: AGES uses a GAL80 fusion protein, which allows the use of the system alongside the majority of existing GAL4-driver lines, whereby suppression of the GAL4-UAS activation is achieved in all cells where auxin is absent.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the manuscript.

claim: AGES will not work with split-GAL4 lines that use a p65 or VP16 activator domain.
source: There are split-GAL4 lines that use the GAL4 activation domain (Luan et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010), however, many use a p65 activator domain (Dionne et al., 2018; Tirian and Dickson, 2017), or a VP16 activator domain (Luan et al., 2006), which will not work with AGES.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of GAL80 inhibition.

claim: AGES demonstrates an almost complete repression of GAL4 activity when un-induced.
source: While some current systems are known to exhibit leaky expression (Scialo et al., 2016), AGES demonstrates an almost complete repression of GAL4 activity when un-induced.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2B and 4.

claim: The AID tags on GAL80 allow the rapid, and tuneable, degradation of the GAL80 protein.
source: The AID tags on GAL80 allow the rapid, and tuneable, degradation of the GAL80 protein, providing users with the option to determine the strength of expression by adjusting the concentration of auxin in the food, or by limiting the exposure time of the flies to auxin.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of the auxin-degron system.

claim: AGES can elicit strong behavioural changes through activating expression of Kir2.1 in PDF-GAL4 expressing adult neurons.
source: We demonstrate that AGES can elicit strong behavioural changes through activating expression of Kir2.1 (an inward-rectifier potassium ion channel) in PDF-GAL4 expressing adult neurons (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Kir2.1 inhibits the activity of PDF neurons resulting in ablation of circadian rhythms.
source: Kir2.1 inhibits the activity of PDF neurons resulting in ablation of circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: 2 mM auxin food had no effect on the circadian rhythm of female flies.
source: While 2 mM auxin food had no effect on the circadian rhythm of female flies (Figure 6D) or the PDF-GAL4/+ control male flies (Figure 6C), it did impact on the UAS-Kir2.1/+ control male flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 2 mM auxin food had no effect on the circadian rhythm of PDF-GAL4/+ control male flies.
source: While 2 mM auxin food had no effect on the circadian rhythm of female flies (Figure 6D) or the PDF-GAL4/+ control male flies (Figure 6C), it did impact on the UAS-Kir2.1/+ control male flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 2 mM auxin food did impact on the UAS-Kir2.1/+ control male flies.
source: While 2 mM auxin food had no effect on the circadian rhythm of female flies (Figure 6D) or the PDF-GAL4/+ control male flies (Figure 6C), it did impact on the UAS-Kir2.1/+ control male flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 10 mM auxin food did have an effect on both male control lines in the circadian rhythm experiment.
source: Also, in this context, 10 mM auxin food did have an effect on both male control lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 10 mM auxin had no impact on adult climbing.
source: So, while 10 mM auxin had no impact on adult climbing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), it did impact on circadian rhythms.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NAA was used for the circadian rhythm experiment, whereas K-NAA was used for all the other experiments.
source: It should be noted that NAA was used for the circadian rhythm experiment, whereas K-NAA (more water soluble) was used for all the other experiments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: K-NAA may have less of an effect on the controls as was seen with NAA.
source: Therefore, K-NAA may have less of an effect on the controls as was seen with NAA.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences.

claim: AGES is a system that is safe for both humans and flies.
source: AGES is also a system that is safe for both humans and flies alike.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of hazardous concerns and lethal effects.

claim: Auxin hormone carries no hazardous concerns for human handling.
source: Auxin hormone carries no hazardous concerns for human handling, and no lethal effects were identified for the effective concentrations of 10 mM or below for both adult and larval stages (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: No lethal effects were identified for the effective concentrations of 10 mM or below auxin for both adult and larval stages.
source: Auxin hormone carries no hazardous concerns for human handling, and no lethal effects were identified for the effective concentrations of 10 mM or below for both adult and larval stages (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Continuous exposure of larvae to 10 mM auxin does result in some developmental delay.
source: Continuous exposure of larvae to 10 mM auxin does result in some developmental delay; however, it does not affect survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Continuous exposure of larvae to 10 mM auxin does not affect survival.
source: Continuous exposure of larvae to 10 mM auxin does result in some developmental delay; however, it does not affect survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Higher concentrations of auxin result in increased mortality rates.
source: Higher concentrations of auxin result in increased mortality rates (data not shown) and should be avoided.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text, though data is not shown.

claim: The recommended use is up to 5 mM auxin for larvae and up to 10 mM for adults for optimal induction.
source: Overall, based on our data, we recommend the use of up to 5 mM auxin and up to 10 mM for optimal induction in larvae and adults, respectively.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the data presented.

claim: Expenses of the GeneSwitch system average £0.31 (GBP) per vial.
source: While expenses of the GeneSwitch system average £0.31 (GBP) per vial, AGES costs ~120× less at £0.0025 per vial (authors' estimate).
evidence: This is an estimate provided by the authors.

claim: AGES costs ~120× less than GeneSwitch at £0.0025 per vial.
source: While expenses of the GeneSwitch system average £0.31 (GBP) per vial, AGES costs ~120× less at £0.0025 per vial (authors' estimate).
evidence: This is an estimate provided by the authors.

claim: Water-soluble auxin (K-NAA) can be easily added to the food immediately before the food is poured into vials or bottles.
source: Furthermore, the water-soluble auxin (K-NAA) can be easily added to the food immediately before the food is poured into vials or bottles, requiring no additional safety measures, enabling ease of production.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: Auxin-containing food can be stored at 4°C for up to 15 weeks where the hormone's potency still persists.
source: In our experience, auxin-containing food can be stored 4°C for up to 15 weeks (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) where the hormone's potency still persists.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The sensitivity of the system is directly related to the amount of auxin present within the tissue.
source: The sensitivity of the system is directly related to the amount of auxin present within the tissue, and thus concerns are raised regarding the fly's age and sex, as these factors impact feeding rates (Carey et al., 2006; Wong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of the system and supported by citations.

claim: Fly's age and sex impact feeding rates.
source: The sensitivity of the system is directly related to the amount of auxin present within the tissue, and thus concerns are raised regarding the fly's age and sex, as these factors impact feeding rates (Carey et al., 2006; Wong et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lower expression is to be expected in older flies.
source: As all experimental adult flies were aged to 5 days post-eclosion, the effects of age on the system are yet to be determined, although lower expression is to be expected in older flies.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known effects of age on feeding.

claim: Limitations of AGES include the response time of the system (18–24 hr).
source: Despite the various advantages that AGES offers the fly community, there are still limitations to consider. These include (i) the response time of the system (18–24 hr), (ii) auxin can have subtle effects on adult behaviour (circadian rhythms), and (iii) induced levels of expression are not always as high as the maximum levels obtained without the system.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: Auxin can have subtle effects on adult behaviour (circadian rhythms).
source: Despite the various advantages that AGES offers the fly community, there are still limitations to consider. These include (i) the response time of the system (18–24 hr), (ii) auxin can have subtle effects on adult behaviour (circadian rhythms), and (iii) induced levels of expression are not always as high as the maximum levels obtained without the system.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Induced levels of expression are not always as high as the maximum levels obtained without the system.
source: Despite the various advantages that AGES offers the fly community, there are still limitations to consider. These include (i) the response time of the system (18–24 hr), (ii) auxin can have subtle effects on adult behaviour (circadian rhythms), and (iii) induced levels of expression are not always as high as the maximum levels obtained without the system.
